title: Central chest discomfort in a 54-year-old man
opening_brief:
You are a medical student working in the emergency department.

A 54-year-old male has presented with chest discomfort.

Your objective is to assess the patient, gather relevant information, identify possible diagnoses, and explain your clinical reasoning.

patient.name: Rajesh Menon
patient.background: Sedentary desk job. Came in with his wife, who insisted.

persona.speech_style: Understates things. Calls it 'discomfort', not pain.
persona.emotional_state: Playing it down, but visibly uneasy and sweaty.
knows_not: the name of his blood pressure tablet, only that it is 'a small white one'
whether his ECG has ever been done before
quirks: Says 'it's probably just gas' if the student pauses too long.

present_illness.onset: Started around 7 this morning while walking to the bus stop.
present_illness.site: Middle of the chest, behind the breastbone.
present_illness.character: A heaviness, like something pressing down. Not sharp.
present_illness.radiation: Sometimes goes into the left arm, and up into the jaw.
present_illness.duration: Comes and goes; the current episode has lasted about 40 minutes.
present_illness.severity: About 6 out of 10 at its worst.
present_illness.timing: Worse in the morning and on any exertion.
present_illness.aggravating: Walking, especially uphill or in a hurry. Also came on after a heavy meal once last week.
present_illness.relieving: Stopping and standing still eases it within a few minutes.
associated: short of breath during the worst episode
present_illness.progression: Similar but milder episodes for about three weeks; today is the worst and the first one that did not settle quickly.

past_medical: High blood pressure, diagnosed about six years ago
Told his blood sugar was 'borderline' at a health check two years ago; no follow-up
No previous heart attack or stroke
medications: One small white blood pressure tablet every morning, takes it most days
An antacid he bought himself, which did not help today
family: Father had a heart attack at 52 and died at 60
Elder brother had a stent put in at 55
social: Smokes 15 cigarettes a day for about 30 years
Drinks alcohol two or three times a week
Works long hours, eats out often
review_of_systems_positive: occasional heartburn after spicy food, but different from this
gained about 6 kg in two years
review_of_systems_negative: no leg swelling or calf pain
no recent travel or long journeys
no vomiting blood or black stools
no pain on pressing the chest wall
no palpitations that he has noticed

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Pulse 96/min regular. BP 156/94 mmHg in the right arm, 152/92 in the left. Respiratory rate 18/min. SpO2 97% on room air. Temperature 36.9 C.

examination.label: General examination
examination.result: Centrally obese, clammy and sweaty. Xanthelasma over both eyelids. No pallor, no cyanosis, no clubbing.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Apex beat in the fifth space, mid-clavicular line, not heaving. Heart sounds S1 and S2 normal, a soft S4 audible. No murmur, no rub, no gallop.

examination.label: Peripheral pulses and BP in both arms
examination.result: All peripheral pulses present and symmetrical. No radio-femoral delay. No inter-arm BP difference beyond 4 mmHg.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.result: Chest clear, equal air entry, no crackles, no wheeze.

examination.label: Chest wall palpation
examination.result: No tenderness on palpation. The discomfort is not reproduced by pressing.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.result: Soft, mild epigastric fullness, no tenderness, no organomegaly.

examination.label: Lower limb examination
examination.result: No calf tenderness, no swelling, no oedema.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: Sinus rhythm at 96/min. Horizontal ST depression of 1.5 mm in leads V4 to V6, with T-wave inversion in II, III and aVF. No ST elevation. No pathological Q waves.

investigations.label: High-sensitivity troponin
investigations.result: Troponin I at presentation 214 ng/L (upper reference limit 34). Repeat at 3 hours: 890 ng/L.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Normal cardiac size. Clear lung fields. Mediastinum not widened.

investigations.label: Fasting lipid profile
investigations.result: Total cholesterol 248 mg/dL, LDL 172 mg/dL, HDL 33 mg/dL, triglycerides 214 mg/dL.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, Na 139, K 4.3 mEq/L.

investigations.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram
investigations.result: Hypokinesia of the mid and apical anterolateral wall. Left ventricular ejection fraction 46%. No pericardial effusion. No aortic dissection flap seen.

investigations.label: D-dimer
investigations.note: Low pre-test probability for pulmonary embolism here; a positive result would only have generated a needless CT.

investigations.label: CT pulmonary angiogram
investigations.result: No pulmonary embolus. No aortic dissection. Incidental hepatic steatosis.
investigations.note: Not indicated with a low Wells score and an ischaemic ECG; delays reperfusion decisions.

investigations.label: Upper GI endoscopy
investigations.note: Never the first move in undifferentiated chest pain with cardiac risk factors.

differentials.why: Exertional retrosternal heaviness radiating to arm and jaw with diaphoresis, on a background of multiple risk factors, with ischaemic ST depression and a rising troponin.
Catastrophic if missed and the treatment is opposite to that of ACS. Argued against by the absence of tearing pain, inter-arm BP difference, pulse deficit or a widened mediastinum.
Another life-threatening cause of chest pain with breathlessness. Low Wells score, no risk factors, normal saturations and no right-heart strain make it unlikely.
The three-week pattern was stable angina; the failure of today's episode to settle and the troponin rise mark the change to an acute coronary syndrome.
The patient's own explanation, and postprandial episodes fit — but reflux is not relieved by rest and does not raise troponin.
No pleuritic or positional pain, no rub, no saddle ST elevation with PR depression.
The pain is not reproducible on palpation and is exertional.

final_diagnosis: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) on a background of crescendo angina, in a patient with hypertension, undiagnosed type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, smoking and a strong family history
diagnosis_reasoning: Exertional retrosternal heaviness radiating to the left arm and jaw, relieved by rest, with diaphoresis and nausea, is textbook ischaemic cardiac pain. The three-week crescendo pattern culminating in a prolonged episode at rest defines an acute coronary syndrome. Ischaemic ST depression without ST elevation, plus a troponin that rises from 214 to 890 ng/L, makes it an NSTEMI rather than unstable angina. Regional hypokinesia on echo in a matching territory confirms it.

history.label: Site of the pain
history.teaching_note: Central retrosternal location is one half of the classic description.

history.label: Character of the pain
history.teaching_note: Heaviness or pressure points to ischaemia; sharp and stabbing points elsewhere.

history.label: Radiation of the pain
history.teaching_note: Radiation to the left arm and jaw roughly doubles the likelihood of an acute coronary syndrome. Radiation to the back would raise dissection instead.

history.label: Onset and timing
history.teaching_note: Duration decides whether this is stable angina or an acute coronary syndrome.

history.label: Aggravating factors, especially exertion
history.teaching_note: Reproducible exertional onset is the single most useful discriminator between cardiac and non-cardiac chest pain.

history.label: Relieving factors
history.teaching_note: Relief within minutes of rest is characteristic of angina.

history.label: Associated autonomic and cardiorespiratory symptoms
history.teaching_note: Diaphoresis, nausea and dyspnoea with chest pain markedly raise the probability of infarction. This is the classic omission in a student history.

history.label: Previous similar episodes
history.teaching_note: A crescendo pattern over weeks is the natural history of an evolving acute coronary syndrome.

history.label: Cardiac risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, lipids
history.teaching_note: Pre-test probability is built from risk factors; without them the ECG and troponin cannot be interpreted properly.

history.label: Smoking history
history.teaching_note: The strongest modifiable risk factor in this age group.

history.label: Family history of premature coronary disease
history.teaching_note: A first-degree relative with coronary disease before 55 is an independent risk factor and is present here.

history.label: Current medication and compliance
history.teaching_note: Poor compliance with antihypertensives explains the uncontrolled BP.

history.label: Risk factors for venous thromboembolism
history.teaching_note: Consciously excluding pulmonary embolism is part of a safe chest-pain history.

history.label: Reflux, indigestion and relation to meals
history.teaching_note: Worth asking, but never enough on its own to discharge a patient with cardiac risk factors.

examination.label: Vital signs, including BP in both arms
examination.teaching_note: An inter-arm difference is the bedside screen for dissection before anticoagulation is given.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.teaching_note: A new murmur would suggest a mechanical complication; a rub would suggest pericarditis.

examination.label: Jugular venous pressure
examination.teaching_note: A raised JVP with clear lungs points to right ventricular infarction or pulmonary embolism.

examination.label: Respiratory examination
examination.teaching_note: Basal crackles would signal Killip class II and change the prognosis.

examination.label: Legs for DVT and oedema
examination.teaching_note: Part of consciously excluding pulmonary embolism.

examination.label: Chest wall palpation
examination.teaching_note: Reproducible tenderness argues for a musculoskeletal cause, though it never excludes ischaemia.

investigations.label: 12-lead ECG
investigations.teaching_note: Must be obtained within 10 minutes of arrival for any adult with chest pain. It is the decision point between STEMI and non-STEMI pathways.

investigations.label: Serial troponin
investigations.teaching_note: A single troponin is not enough; the rise and fall over 3 hours is what distinguishes infarction from a chronically elevated baseline.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.teaching_note: Screens for a widened mediastinum, pneumothorax and pulmonary oedema.

investigations.label: Blood glucose and HbA1c
investigations.teaching_note: Uncovers the undiagnosed diabetes driving his risk.

investigations.label: Lipid profile
investigations.teaching_note: Needed for secondary prevention, and best taken early in the admission.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.teaching_note: Determines contrast safety before angiography and guides drug dosing.

investigations.label: Echocardiogram
investigations.teaching_note: Regional wall-motion abnormality localises the infarct and quantifies ventricular function.

hints: Go back to what the patient told you about when the discomfort comes on and what makes it stop.
Think about conditions in which symptoms appear on exertion and settle with rest, and what that pattern implies about supply and demand.
Review the structured approach to acute chest pain: the three diagnoses that must be excluded before anything else, and how the ECG and troponin separate them.
teaching_points: Exertional retrosternal heaviness with radiation to the arm or jaw, relieved by rest and accompanied by diaphoresis, is ischaemic until proven otherwise, whatever the patient calls it.
Every adult with chest pain needs an ECG within 10 minutes, and troponin measured serially rather than once.
Aortic dissection must be excluded before anticoagulating: ask about tearing pain radiating to the back, check both arms, look at the mediastinum.
A normal initial troponin never excludes an acute coronary syndrome; a normal ECG never excludes one either.
The absence of chest-wall tenderness does not confirm cardiac pain, but its presence does not exclude it.
